Volunteers walked in braces set to different neck shapes while a treadmill jolted them or while they stepped sideways to a target.

Jolts shrank stability in all conditions, but only braced walking tipped into measured instability in one direction. Side stepping stayed accurate except when the brace bent the neck forward and the target lay far away. The authors advise fall risk teaching for people given neck immobilisation.
plos-pone-0354425:
Fumiyo Nakagawa led a team of eight authors mapping how people who live with HIV in Britain use health services, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. With good treatment, HIV is now a long-term condition, but not everyone uses services equally. The team compared use across social and demographic groups.

Nakagawa's patterns reveal who is underserved, by age, background, or circumstance. Unequal use can mean missed chances to keep the virus suppressed and catch other illnesses early. The NHS aims for equal care, so maps like this show where outreach must reach further. The study gives service planners UK-specific evidence instead of assumptions imported from other health systems.
plos-pone-0354525:
De Herdt and colleagues, in 2026, study a drug target that may help repair myelin, the coating that speeds signals along nerve fibers. Loss of myelin is a core harm in multiple sclerosis. A receptor called GPR17 stays switched on in young myelin-making cells after injury, and that may block them from maturing.

The team first checked human brain tissue from people with multiple sclerosis and found more of these receptor-marked cells near damaged areas. They then gave mice with toxin-caused myelin loss a new drug that blocks GPR17 by mouth. Treated mice showed faster repair in key brain and optic nerve areas. Their memory and visual signals also recovered. The results point to blocking this receptor as a possible route toward repair-focused treatment, though the work is still in animals.
plos-pone-0354725:
Mushuai Hao, Haonan Qi, Liang Zhao, and Wei Han published this 2026 training study on how the lowering speed of a squat shapes strength gains. Thirty sports students trained twice weekly for eight weeks at one of three tempos: a slow four-second lowering, a two-second lowering, or a self-chosen rhythm. Strength, sprinting, and jumping were tested before and after.

All groups grew stronger, and the two-second tempo showed the friendliest trend, boosting explosive jumping most. The slow group actually lost some spring-based explosiveness despite gaining strength. Hao advises matching tempo to the quality being trained.
plos-pone-0354825:
Uchhwas Banik and five colleagues published this 2026 study turning waste plastic into fuel in Bangladesh, where plastic use keeps climbing. They heated four common plastics without oxygen, a process called pyrolysis, and tuned the temperature for each type to draw off the most liquid oil and char.

Polypropylene gave the richest oil yield, and the liquids resembled familiar fuels in their carbon makeup. The leftover char was checked for industrial uses as well. Banik presents tuned pyrolysis as a practical route for cutting plastic waste while recovering energy from it.
plos-pone-0354925:
Lixia Lin and five colleagues published this 2026 plant study on a valued Chinese medicinal herb that wilts in heat. They grew the plant at four temperatures, from mild to severely hot, and tracked leaf health, chemistry, and protein changes to see how it copes and where it fails.

Heat cut photosynthesis, lowered green pigment, and raised signs of cell damage. Hundreds of proteins shifted, including ones for daily rhythms, antioxidant defense, and the cell's recycling system, which seemed to protect tissue. Lin's findings give breeders and growers a starting map for raising heat tolerance in a crop that warming summers now threaten.
plos-pone-0355125:
Victoria Ballén led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of drug-resistant E. coli in Barcelona's water treatment plants. They collected well over a hundred resistant strains across two wastewater plants and one drinking water plant, then read their genomes and tested drug resistance, film-forming ability, and virulence genes.

Treatment lowered bacteria counts, yet most strains still resisted several drugs, and some dangerous clones survived into reclaimed water. One resistant strain even appeared at the drinking water plant's inlet. Ballén argues water systems belong inside resistance surveillance, not outside it.
plos-pone-0355625:
Masaaki Kuwajima and colleagues built a new lab animal for brain research: a rat missing a protein called synaptopodin. Their 2026 paper explains that the protein helps organize tiny structures inside nerve cells that support learning signals. Mice without it existed already, but rats offer steadier timing for when learning circuits switch on, which can make experiments cleaner.

The engineered rats lived and kept normal kidney function, though they grew slightly smaller than usual. Under strong microscopes, their brain cells lacked two small internal structures that depend on the protein, and a key learning signal in the memory region ran weaker. Kuwajima and co-authors present the rat as a shared tool for studying growth, behavior, and memory.
plos-pone-0355725:
Li-Feng Hung and four colleagues track drug-resistant gut bacteria in emergency department patients across the rise and fall of Taiwan's COVID-19 Omicron wave, in this 2026 study. Their hospital's records covered more than eight hundred adults with bloodstream infections from a bacterial family that includes E. coli, about a third of them multidrug-resistant. The team divided the year into pre-peak, peak, and post-peak stages and searched broadly for stage-specific risk factors.

Which variables accompanied resistance changed with the stage: advanced age and red-cell measures early on, liver and platelet values at the peak, and white-cell measures afterward. Resistance trends also split by species, one notorious pathogen gaining ground against a key antibiotic while E. coli's resistance eased against several drugs. The authors argue stewardship and risk checks should adapt as a pandemic moves through its phases.
plos-pone-0356725:
Dipo Aldila and coauthors published a 2026 mathematical modeling study in PLOS ONE on hepatitis B and D, two linked liver viruses. Hepatitis D cannot spread on its own; it infects only people already carrying hepatitis B, through what is called superinfection, and it makes outcomes far worse. Their model splits a population into susceptible, vaccinated, infected, recovered, chronic, and doubly infected groups, with vaccination and liver transplantation as controls.

The analysis shows familiar threshold behavior: when the basic reproduction number sits below one, the disease-free state is stable and infection dies out. Above it, two kinds of settled states appear, with and without hepatitis D. A global sensitivity analysis found vaccination coverage and vaccine strength dominate that threshold number. Transplantation does not move the threshold, but it shrinks outbreaks and delays their peaks. Vaccine effort, they argue, is the master lever, with transplantation buying time and sparing severe cases.
plos-pone-0356825:
Ravian Wettstein and colleagues follow adults with attention deficit disorder for years. Their trial had added talking therapy to medication and education. The question now is whether the therapy pays off late, in quality of life. Early results had shown no added benefit right after treatment, but coping skills might ripen slowly. From the original cohort of several hundred, about a quarter completed the long follow-up survey several years later, rating life quality on a standard scale.

Life quality rose sharply by the end of the original treatment in both groups, then eased back over the years while staying above the starting point. No measure separated the therapy group from the education-only group at any point. Wettstein and colleagues conclude this dataset gives no sign of a delayed therapy dividend, though early gains themselves partly lasted.
plos-pone-0357025:
Marjolijn Carolien Sales and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on predicting right heart failure after a patient receives a durable left ventricular assist device, a heart pump. When the heart's right side fails after surgery, patients can crash, so surgeons lean on risk scores rarely validated head to head. They applied six established scores to just over a hundred patients at one center, using a standard registry definition.

About one patient in five developed moderate-to-severe right heart failure. The established scores discriminated weakly to moderately; one scored worse than chance, while a postoperative version performed best of them. An exploratory five-variable model built by the team, using sickness level, liver markers, and pressure measurements, appeared much stronger, and held up after internal bootstrap checks. Derived and tested in the same small cohort, it needs outside validation before any clinical use.
plos-pone-0357125:
Hanizah Mohd Yusoff and coauthors published a 2026 nationwide survey in PLOS ONE on how Long COVID harms the working lives of factory workers in Malaysia. Close to eight hundred workers who had previously caught COVID filled in questionnaires on lingering symptoms, quality of working life, productivity, and safety. The authors then looked for which personal, symptom, job, and workplace factors tracked with poor work outcomes.

About a quarter of workers with Long COVID reported poor quality of working life. Roughly two in five admitted working while sick, about one in eight had taken sickness absences, and a small share reported safety problems. Risk rose with older age, smoking, more symptoms, shift work, chemical handling, confined spaces, noise, and manual lifting. Factories without a sickness absence policy fared markedly worse. The authors argue employers need formal absence policies and hazard controls aimed at this group, not just general wellness advice.
plos-pone-0357625:
Anqi Hu and seven colleagues compare gut microbes in giant pandas that pace and sway repetitively with those that do not, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Such stereotypic behavior troubles captive pandas, and gut microbes are known to influence the brain in other animals. The team watched fifteen captive pandas, then sequenced the bacteria in their droppings using two methods to build both a species list and a functional profile.

Pandas showing the behavior carried a distinctly different gut community, a pattern the authors describe as imbalance. One Serratia species was far more common in them, several Clostridium species trended upward, and a friendly Enterococcus species went the other way. Some of the shifted bacteria touch pathways that make brain signaling chemicals. The panda findings cannot prove cause, but they open a new angle on managing a stubborn welfare problem in zoos.
plos-pone-0357725:
Carla Blázquez-Fernández, Paloma Lanza-León, and David Cantarero-Prieto published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on social isolation and health behavior across generations in Europe. Isolation is a known health risk in old age, but its effects on the young are barely studied. Using the latest European Social Survey from twenty-four countries. The authors related five isolation measures, from rarely meeting others to lacking emotional support, against inactivity, smoking, drinking, and body weight. They did this generation by generation.

Isolation tracked with worse health behavior in every generation. Rarely meeting socially, for instance, raised the odds of physical inactivity across all ages. Generation X appeared as a bridge group, mixing traditional and modern patterns of connection and habit. Anti-isolation policy, they argue, should be age-specific and start young, because disconnection's health costs accumulate across a lifetime; social connection itself is preventive medicine.
plos-pone-0358125:
Jingwang Liu led a team of eight authors testing a drug's protective effect in mice, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. When blood flow returns to a limb cut off from circulation, the return itself injures muscle, a harm called ischemia-reperfusion injury. The team tested esketamine, a drug already used in clinics, against that injury.

Liu's group found that esketamine protected skeletal muscle in the mouse model. They linked the effect to regulation of autophagy, the cell's cleanup and recycling process. A drug already in human use is an attractive candidate, since its safety record is known. Much testing remains, but the finding hints that surgical patients could one day get muscle protection from a familiar drug.
plos-pone-0358225:
Asha Z Goodman, Winston T Stauffer, and Philippe A Gallay test a two drug bet against the worst outcomes of fatty liver disease, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The logic pairs correction with repair: semaglutide, the metabolic drug, against weight and sugar, plus a cyclophilin inhibitor aimed at the inflammation and scarring that become self sustaining. Their mice developed the disease on a Western diet with sugar water and a liver toxin. Then each group received one drug alone, or both together.

The pairing's effects diverged by outcome, as the design half expected. Semaglutide clearly cut body weight and shrank the liver tumor burden, the cancer endpoint that matters most. Scar tissue, measured by collagen staining, did not differ significantly between the treatment groups. The authors report the split honestly: metabolic victory, fibrosis stalemate. Advanced liver disease may need the scar targeted earlier, harder, or by other means than these.
plos-pone-0358325:
Yeliz Yilmaz Bozok and three colleagues compared two AI chatbots answering breast cancer questions, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Patients increasingly ask chatbots about their disease, so the quality of those answers matters. The team put patient-oriented questions to both ChatGPT and Gemini and scored the replies.

Bozok's head-to-head comparison tells patients and doctors which system gave safer and more accurate answers in this test. It also shows where both systems fell short, which is just as useful. Clinics fielding patient questions about AI use gain grounded advice here. The wider lesson is that chatbot answers on cancer should be checked, and studies like this show how to check them.
plos-pone-0358425:
Rebaka Pradhan and Onn Shehory review what computing research has done about labor trafficking online, in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. Traffickers now recruit and coordinate through digital platforms, while traces of offline exploitation also sit in online records. The authors separate those two settings and ask which machine learning and analytics methods have been tried in each, and where the gaps lie.

Following standard scoping review practice, they searched six databases plus extra sources and screened more than two thousand records down to twenty-one articles worth mapping. Work clusters around online recruitment fraud, illicit massage businesses, supply chains, and high risk industries such as fishing. Case studies, readable classifiers, and topic modeling appear often. Their closing agenda points future researchers toward the neglected settings and data types.
plos-pone-0359425: Cao and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on reading feelings from behavior signals. Their method joins two ideas: injecting extra hub nodes into a graph as behavior unfolds, and fusing the streams with graph attention. The task is multimodal sentiment analysis, judging mood from several signal types at once. Systems that read mood well could support mental health tools and more responsive machines.
plos-pone-0359525:
Zena Abdul-Ameer Mahdi and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It investigates plant chemicals from Rhizophora mucronata, a mangrove tree. The question is whether these phytochemicals can block proteins linked to lung cancer, acting as inhibitors that slow the disease's machinery.

The approach is computational, using multiscale and in silico analyses, meaning computer simulations at several levels rather than wet-lab tests. Screening mangrove compounds on a computer is a cheap first pass for drug hunting. If any candidate looks strong, laboratory teams can test it in cells. Natural product researchers are the readers for this early-stage evidence.
plos-pone-0359625: López-González and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on spotting risky drinking in Guaviare, Colombia. They adapted the AUDIT, a standard alcohol screening survey, for primary care with mixed cultural groups. The team checked that the adapted questions read clearly and made sense to local users. A screening tool that fits local speech can catch alcohol harm earlier across Latin America.
pmc-13197425:
Jacob L Bongers and colleagues used ancient DNA to trace migration on Peru's Pacific coast in a 2026 study. Genome data came from twenty-one people buried in the Chincha Valley of southern Peru. The valley was ruled by the Chincha Kingdom from the thirteenth century until the Inca takeover in the fifteenth.

The DNA shows shared ancestry with groups far to the north. Early migrants carried pure northern ancestry, while later generations mixed with nearby coastal people. Kin buried in a shared family tomb married within the group. A dating model handled diet effects that blur age estimates on this coast. Customs such as skull shaping and red pigment use persisted across those centuries.
pmc-13200325:
Shunsuke Mori and colleagues present a 2026 report on two cases of an abnormal lung artery supply, with a literature review. In this rare condition, a body artery feeds the base of a lung instead of the usual lung artery. Saving lung tissue is favored now, but kept lung can die if mishandled, and selection rules were vague.

Detailed scans guided tailored care for each woman. In one, an aberrant artery held a large clot and the normal artery was undergrown, so surgeons removed just that lung segment by robot. She left hospital on day six. In the other, normal branches were intact, so a coil block of the aberrant artery sufficed. She went home on day three. Neither had complications.
pmc-13202125:
Permanent organ damage accumulates quietly in Sjögren's disease, and a 2026 cohort analysis authored by Onorina Berardicurti charts that accrual over five years. The research article follows 429 adults in an Italian multicentre research network, measuring irreversible damage across eye, mouth, and systemic domains with a validated damage index.

Nearly half the patients already had some damage at baseline, and the share rose to about two thirds after five years of follow-up. Higher baseline disease activity predicted damage in every domain, while an abnormal tear test specifically forecast eye damage. Antibodies, inflammation markers, and repeated mouth infections added domain-specific risks, pointing to earlier monitoring for high-risk patients.
pmc-13202525:
Quieting microbe chatter instead of killing microbes is the strategy in a 2026 study by Kosana Sai Chaitanya against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The research article designs triazole-linked compounds carrying a thiolactone unit to block quorum sensing, the chemical chatter that builds biofilms and drives toxin making.

A library of thirty glycinate and propanoate derivatives was modeled against the LasR regulator protein, then synthesized and tested on a reporter strain. Blocking was strongest at high doses and faded as doses dropped across the tested range. One nitrophenyl compound stood out, disrupting biofilms and cutting output of the pigment pyocyanin, which supports anti-virulence therapy as a complement to antibiotics.
pmc-13204325:
Snacking has quietly replaced meals for many young adults, and a 2026 longitudinal study authored by Mariëlle Tamara de Vaal follows that habit through a phone app. The FOODLOOP study tracked 264 Dutch millennials on twelve nonconsecutive days spread across four seasons, logging each snack's product, setting, and motive.

Participants averaged about four and a half snacks daily, and most choices were relatively healthful items like coffee, tea, fruit, and bread products. Liking, appetite, hunger, convenience, and pleasure drove most snacking, which clustered at home, with other people, and in the afternoon. Millennials with children snacked more than those without, and older millennials snacked more than younger ones.
pmc-13236725:
Salim and colleagues ask whether blood-thinning drugs raise bleeding risk in people with cavernous malformations in the brain. These tangled vessel clusters can bleed into the brain, so doctors often fear prescribing antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs to patients who have them. Hard evidence for that fear has been lacking, leaving hard calls in stroke and heart care.

Using a large health records platform, the team matched patients with these malformations who took blood thinners against similar patients who did not. None had bled before. Comparing later brain bleeds between matched groups gives the fairest test short of a trial, and the answer can free needed treatment.
pmc-13237925:
Huston and colleagues test whether stimulating nerves through the ear can prime the blood to clot faster. In animals, vagus nerve stimulation reduces bleeding after injury. The signal runs through immune cells in the spleen, which raise calcium inside platelets, readying them to activate the moment tissue is torn and clots are needed.

Healthy volunteers received ear-based vagus stimulation, alone or combined with trigeminal nerve stimulation. The team then measured platelet function and standard clotting tests. A safe, wearable way to prime clotting could matter in surgery and trauma, where minutes of bleeding decide outcomes. First, though, the effect must be shown in people, as here.
pmc-13238925:
Handke and colleagues ask whether obesity helps or harms patients treated for advanced urological cancers. Extra weight is reshaping outcomes across oncology in surprising ways. Their study covers metastatic bladder, kidney, and prostate cancers, the three big cancers of the urinary and male reproductive systems, in patients given systemic drug therapy at one high-volume centre.

Looking back over cases treated from 2017 to 2025, the team compares survival between patients with and without obesity. Cancer doctors know this as the obesity paradox question: heavier patients sometimes live longer on modern drugs. A centre-level answer helps clinicians counsel patients honestly instead of assuming weight only ever works against them.
pmc-13242125:
Schöneberg's team in Frankfurt sequenced every type specimen of a Bolivian frog whose home was logged before it was named. Oreobates chiquitanus survives at three sites in the Chiquitano Dry Forest, all near active logging. A base genome came from one paratype; side genomes covered all types. The museum stores became a genetic time capsule.

History rebuilt from genes shows the population rebounding from a dip some three hundred thousand years ago. Gene variety suggests a still-healthy gene pool. Every known population sits beside logging sites all the same. The genomes now anchor a starting line for tracking future genetic erosion.
pmc-13242325:
Hyera's team at the Western Cape bathed fat cells in gold specks to block lipid storage. The work stayed in cell dishes. Citrate-capped particles of fourteen nanometres were made by simple chemistry. Mature mouse fat cells received rising doses. Staining, survival assays, and gene activity arrays tracked the response.

The particles spared cell survival while cutting cell lipid build-up dose by dose. 35 genes shifted, clustered around fat formation and lipid handling. Networks centered on PPAR signaling and fat-cell hub genes. Hyera pitches the gold particles as an obesity play awaiting animal tests.
pmc-13246525:
Smith, Jin, Miller, and co-authors built reference samples for testing milk for bird flu, in this 2026 Food and Environmental Virology paper. With highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 turning up in dairy cattle, laboratories need to detect the virus in milk, and proficiency exercises check whether labs get the right answers. That requires spiked milk samples whose virus levels are known precisely and stay uniform.

The team used digital PCR to count viral genomes in their stock and samples exactly, then confirmed the standard USDA detection assay read them consistently. Replicate samples barely varied, no milk-matrix interference appeared, and levels stayed stable over time. Such well-characterized samples, they argue, make nationwide lab evaluations trustworthy.
pmc-13246925:
Pelzer, Werthmann, and Svaldi piloted mirror exposure therapy for teenagers with anorexia nervosa in this 2026 Eating and Weight Disorders study. Distorted body image drives the illness, and guided sessions viewing oneself in a mirror reduce that distortion in adults, but evidence in adolescents was thin. Twenty-four female inpatients were randomized to twelve mirror sessions over four weeks or to usual treatment alone.

Mirror exposure added no measurable benefit on overall body image or eating-disorder symptoms; both groups improved during inpatient care anyway. Exploratory analyses hinted the mirror group reduced body-checking and avoidance behaviors, and eye tracking confirmed patients fixated on body parts they disliked, though that bias did not shift. The authors say larger trials must find which patients benefit and when.
pmc-13248325:
Ramadanov and colleagues built a prediction model for blood transfusion around hip replacement surgery, reported in 2026. Transfusions after this operation link to worse outcomes and higher costs, yet clinics lacked a tool built for this procedure. The team drew on a registry from one certified German arthroplasty center covering 2016 to 2023.

Of six hundred forty-eight patients, about one in six needed a transfusion. Low starting hemoglobin, longer operating time, greater blood loss, and lower body weight each raised the risk, while male sex lowered it. The model sorted patients accurately, and the authors ask for testing at other hospitals before routine use.
pmc-13248825:
Silveira and a Brazilian team built an antibacterial wound dressing, reported in Small Science in 2026. Infection is the most common reason skin wounds stall, so the team made zinc oxide nanoparticles using moringa leaf extract as fuel. They spun those particles into a membrane of two biodegradable plastics using an electric field method called electrospinning.

The best membrane, holding five percent nanoparticles, soaked up more than three times its weight in fluid and stayed friendly to skin cells in culture. It also held back two common wound bacteria, Staphylococcus aureus and E. coli. The authors propose the dressing for infected and slow-healing wounds, pending further testing.
pmc-13249725:
Valentine, Zhang, and Liu measured how attention treats shapes, in a 2026 perception study. When people attend to a simple feature like color, nearby feature values get a boost that fades with distance, a pattern called similarity gain. The team asked whether the same holds for shape, using a circular shape space where forms morph gradually into one another.

Volunteers watched two target shapes and ignored overlapping distractors, reporting brightness changes in the targets only. Accuracy peaked when the two targets matched and fell steadily as their shapes diverged, across two experiments with different shape ranges. The authors read this as shape-similarity gain: attention boosts look-alike shapes, suggesting the brain keeps an inner similarity map for objects.
pmc-13250225:
Iwu-Jaja and colleagues map research on fighting drug-resistant infections across the World Health Organization's African region. Their 2026 BMJ Public Health scoping review sorts interventions against the five goals of the global action plan on antimicrobial resistance. The team searched four databases, plus grey sources, in late 2025.

Forty-nine studies qualified, clustered in South Africa, Ethiopia, Kenya, Ghana, and Nigeria. Most tested stewardship programs or awareness training in large hospitals and showed better prescribing or knowledge, but few tracked long-term change. Prevention, vaccination, animal-health links, and full cost studies were all scarce in the literature. The authors call for longer implementation research, wider country coverage, and economic analysis to guide the region's response.
pmc-13250325:
Martin Larisch and colleagues tell a cautionary trauma story in this 2026 case report. A 57-year-old woman was in a car crash and developed a severe tear in her small bowel, but since she was stable, she chose treatment without surgery.

Scans three weeks later suggested the tear had healed. At 21 weeks she returned with worsening belly pain, nausea, and vomiting, and imaging showed a new hole at the same spot. Surgery found a three-centimetre tear beside a scarred, narrowed section, and part of the bowel was removed. The authors warn that a healed-looking scan can hide slow blood-starvation damage, so long follow-up is vital.
pmc-13250425:
Matsumoto and colleagues check whether adding bone cement makes hip fracture nails hold better in older patients. Their 2026 Geriatric Orthopaedic Surgery and Rehabilitation study followed three hundred patients at several Japanese centers. All had upper thighbone fractures fixed with a nail inside the bone, with or without cement support.

No screw cut-out, the main failure being tracked, occurred in the cement group, while four cases appeared without cement. Excess sliding of the screw and overall complications were also numerically less common with cement. No cement-related harm was seen during the study period. Differences were not statistically firm, so the authors call the approach promising for high-risk elderly patients and ask for randomized trials.
pmc-13250625:
Ashish Sapkota and colleagues report an unusual concealment case in this 2026 paper. A 28-year-old man was brought from police custody with rectal pain, and after first denying it, he admitted he had hidden six glass drug ampoules inside his rectum.

Examination and imaging confirmed the objects were there. Glass drug vials are fragile, so leakage was a real danger, and surgery was planned. Before it happened, the ampoules passed out on their own with no harm, confirmed by later imaging. The authors note that in stable patients, laxatives and watchful waiting can sometimes avoid surgery, though this lucky ending is not a care plan.
pmc-13250825:
Tachikawa and colleagues report an elderly woman whose colon cancer triggered a dangerous immune overreaction called hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Their 2026 Surgical Case Reports paper covers a syndrome where a cytokine storm drives immune cells to devour blood cells. It usually follows blood cancers, and solid tumors like colon cancer rarely cause it.

The eighty-three-year-old woman arrived with a month of appetite loss, lasting fever, and mental decline. Scans and biopsy found an advanced cancer of the ascending colon, and surgeons removed the right side of her colon robotically. Fever and swelling returned after surgery, and a blood smear on day twenty-five confirmed the syndrome. Stronger steroid treatment failed to help, and she died on day forty-six, leading the authors to urge vigilance for this complication.
pmc-13251825:
Kai Kopecky and a large team study how dead giants shape living ecosystems in this 2026 paper. Foundation species such as trees, grasses, corals, and oysters build whole habitats, and their remains keep working long after death.

The team drew on experiments and records from ten sites across the United States research network. Five sites were on land and five were marine, and the records spanned two to 32 years. The dead routinely changed the life rates of their living kin. Effects ran from halving growth to a twelve-fold rise. The authors call this material legacy a hidden layer of ecosystem memory. They see it as a practical tool as climate-driven die-offs grow.
pmc-13252725:
Calvin Teahan, Enda Whyte, and Siobhán O'Connor survey Gaelic games coaches on injury prevention in this 2026 study. Ireland's fast, evasive field sports injure legs often, and warm-up exercise programmes proven to cut injuries exist, yet word was that few coaches used them.

Of 342 adult coaches answering an anonymous online survey, about six in ten used some form of prevention routine, but only 44 percent knew the formal programmes. Elite coaches used them more than others. Many coaches built or tweaked their own versions. Attitudes were positive, but four in ten admitted they did not know how to run a programme, and a third said no training was available. Education is the fix proposed.
pmc-13253825:
Akira Shinaoka and co-authors test a citrus compound on lymph flow in a 2026 trial. Monoglucosyl hesperidin, from citrus peel, aids blood flow and cuts swelling in earlier work. Thirty healthy adults took 300 milligrams a day or a placebo, swapping over in a crossover design, while scans measured the main lymph duct.

No effect showed in the full group. Among people with no exercise habit, though, the duct widened clearly after intake, matching higher lymph flow seen in animal studies. The authors also propose duct scans as a painless marker for future lymph studies.
pmc-13254625: Viet Thuc Dang and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to their paper on a bis-macrocyclic peptide ligand designed to mimic the active site of multicopper oxidase enzymes. The correction fixes two errors. One is the affiliation listing for author Andy Nguyen, which should be only the University of Illinois Chicago. The other is a misspelling of the word macrocyclic in the original title. The publisher apologizes for the errors, and no findings of the study are changed in this notice.
pmc-13260025:
Simone Treccarichi leads a 2026 genetics case study of a newly found variant in a gene called RAPGEF6. A variant is a change in a gene's code, and de novo means it appeared new in this person rather than being inherited. The patient had psychiatric disorders and mild intellectual disability. Trio-based whole-exome sequencing, which reads the protein-coding genes of a patient and both parents, found the change.

The variant shifts the reading frame of the gene and was classed as likely disease-causing under standard criteria. Evidence suggests it triggers destruction of the gene's message, so little protein is made. Brain data show the gene is active across the whole lifespan and rises as nerve cells mature in lab tests. The authors argue that having only one working copy contributes to developmental and psychiatric problems.
pmc-13260725:

pmc-13293425:
Adding one bacterial type to larval water is the change Camden M. Dezse and colleagues tested in a 2026 study of adult male Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. Males are mass-reared for release programs that suppress wild mosquito numbers, so adult quality matters greatly.

Of three bacterial isolates tried in normal rearing water, one, a Cedecea species, slowed the shift to pupae and gave adult males with shorter wings and shorter lives. The other isolates did not show that harm. Small shifts in larval microbes can thus echo through adult life. Rearing centers may need to watch water microbes closely to keep release males fit.
pmc-13293625:
Tomoyasu Kashiwagi and colleagues report, in a 2026 surgical case, a strangulated small bowel blockage tangled with a major pelvic artery after lymph node surgery. A 77-year-old man arrived with severe belly pain after earlier bladder surgery.

Scans showed a closed loop of bowel with suspected blood cutoff near the right external iliac artery. At emergency surgery, dead bowel filled the right pelvis, and gentle freeing failed. Surgeons cut within the dead segment first to ease tension and see clearly, then found the artery as the pinching structure. About 230 centimeters of bowel were removed, the artery was saved, and recovery was smooth.
pmc-13293725:
Wenwen Liang and colleagues model, in a 2026 study, what predicts recovery from depression after stroke, a common and harmful complication. Mood after stroke swings between recovery and relapse, yet what drives each shift was unclear.

A time-based model followed 536 patients with blocked-artery stroke across 1441 check-ins, sorting them into no, mild, and severe depression states. Moves from mild depression back to none were 5.5 times more likely than moves to severe states, a ratio the authors report. Schooling of ten years or more cut worsening risk, while independence and social support favored recovery. Severe spells looked brief, though missing death data cloud that finding.
pmc-13293825:
Led by Milena Wojciechowska, a 2026 study asks which mental traits shape daily life for people living with asthma. Patients were compared with healthy controls. The team used scales for functioning in chronic illness, asthma control, self-esteem, illness acceptance, and depression, then tested which factors predicted how well patients coped.

Overall functioning in the asthma group was moderate. Acceptance of illness and self-esteem were the strongest predictors, mainly for emotional and social life. Weaker mental resources and more depressive symptoms went with poorer functioning. Poor asthma control also tended to track with worse daily functioning, which argues for routine mental health checks in asthma care.
pmc-13293925:
Qian Li and a large team build a deep learning tool in 2026 to predict heavy lymph node spread in esophageal squamous cell cancer before surgery. Standard CT rules based on node size miss many cases. Their model first learned from 3,200 unlabeled chest scans, then trained on tumor volumes from 1,060 patients across two centers with later and outside test groups.

Accuracy held up well across checks, with area values of 0.881 inside, 0.860 over time, and 0.860 externally. In the outside group, sensitivity beat a guideline-style comparator while specificity also rose. Better calibration adds trust. Such prediction could sharpen staging and treatment choices before an operation.
pmc-13294325:
Sílvia Rocha and coauthors review fat tissue growth and remodeling in a 2026 article on obesity targets. Making new fat cells, called adipogenesis, follows gene cascades led by PPAR gamma and C/EBP proteins, tuned by Wnt, bone morphogenetic protein, and insulin signals. Healthy expansion stores fat safely and renews tissue.

In obesity, excess nutrients and hormone shifts stall healthy cell creation. Existing cells swell instead, oxygen drops, inflammation lingers, and fat spills into organs, driving insulin resistance and heart-metabolic disease. Guiding growth toward fresh, well-behaved fat cells rather than swollen ones is framed as a promising route to restore balance.
pmc-13295925:
Takayuki Ando and co-authors examine, in 2026, why people with several chronic conditions end up attending many clinics in Japan, a pattern called polydoctoring. Using nationwide claims data, they track what changes when a new condition appears in the same person.

Nearly 4.7 million adults were followed, and every new condition added clinic ties, but by very different amounts. Cancer raised the count most, followed by osteoporosis and arthritis, while effects shrank among the oldest patients and those already carrying many conditions. The authors say care coordination should be tailored by condition, not one-size-fits-all.
pmc-13296225:
Jessica Hui and colleagues review, in 2026, breast findings spotted by chance on chest scans at their institution over two years. They track how often such findings appear in women over forty, what radiologists recommend and what follow-up actually happens.

Findings turned up in about one in seven scans, and dedicated breast imaging was advised in a small share of cases. Where workup happened, most results were harmless and only four cancers emerged. Wording mattered: firm recommendations led to follow-up far more often than optional phrasing. The authors call for standard reporting and follow-up rules.
pmc-13297725: Denis Bignotti and his co-authors issued a short fix to their 2026 case series on Class II bite care with bar devices and clear aligners. The fix adds a thanks section that was left out of the first print run. It thanks the Centro Ortodontico Vicentino and its head, Leonella Caliari, for their help, skill, and support through the work. The authors state the science in the paper stands as it was, and an editor signed off on the change.
pmc-13297925:
A heart scan lit up the stomach and thyroid gland but left the bones dark. That odd spread told Hiroyuki Tokue and his team the tracer dose was faulty, not the patient. Their 2026 case report tells of a 75-year-old woman with kidney disease and a slow heart rhythm, scanned for feared amyloid in the heart.

The dye left no real mark in heart muscle. Its pattern matched free pertechnetate loose in the body, a sign of a mixing or dosing slip with the technetium dose. A fresh scan 1.5 months later spread through bone as it should. It again showed no amyloid. The team warns that scans with this pattern must be read as failed tests, not as clean bills of health.
pmc-13298225:
Every day's coffee habit leaves mountains of grounds behind, and Sreehitha Pilli with colleagues review how to turn that waste into products in a 2026 article. Spent coffee grounds, produced in millions of tonnes yearly, still hold caffeine, fiber, antioxidants, proteins, and oils worth recovering.

The review surveys pretreatment, green extraction, and bioconversion routes feeding food, nutraceutical, bioenergy, and packaging uses, with multi-product biorefineries as the goal. Scaling up remains hard: the grounds vary in composition, processing eats energy, and safety testing lags behind enthusiasm. The authors call for standardized characterization, pilot-scale trials, and AI-assisted process tuning to make commercial upcycling realistic.
pmc-13298525:
Small flesh-colored bumps on a young man's penis turned out to be a benign nerve tumor, describe Phatcharawat Chirasuthat and colleagues in a 2026 case report. The 23-year-old had three firm papules on the glans that grew slowly over three years, mildly itchy but causing no urinary or sexual symptoms.

Removal and microscopy showed a neatly bounded dermal nodule of spindle cells in interlacing bundles, and staining confirmed Schwann cell origin with S-100 positivity. The diagnosis was palisaded encapsulated neuroma, a harmless growth with no known risk of turning malignant. The authors note that complete excision both settles the diagnosis and cures the lesion, with no recurrence expected.
pmc-13302725:
Routine protein levels sketch a COVID-19 patient's road ahead, Rauno Joks and colleagues report in a 2026 chart review. Of 569 adults hospitalized with COVID-19 pneumonia, sixty had the full laboratory and immune data the analysis required. Albumin, globulin, and their ratio were tested against comorbidity burden, predicted ten-year survival, severity scores, and length of stay.

Low albumin and a low albumin-to-globulin ratio each tracked with heavier comorbidity, lower predicted survival, and longer hospitalization, independent of other factors. Falling total protein meant higher severity scores. Globulin alone predicted nothing. The authors propose these cheap, standard tests as aids for sorting patients by likely course and recovery.
pmc-13303925:
Mohammad Hussein Mustafa and colleagues map research on artificial intelligence for hospital infection work in a 2026 scoping review. Software has been proposed to spot infections, sort patient risk, and guide antibiotic choices, but strong proof of patient benefit remains unclear.

Six databases were searched under standard scoping guidance, and 39 studies qualified from hundreds screened. Nearly all work built or tested models on past data, with no randomized trials and few fair tests under everyday ward conditions. Surgical wound and urinary infections drew most attention. The authors warn against reading lab accuracy as proof of clinical value.
pmc-13304125:
Kasim Akay leads a 2026 study testing whether a simple blood ratio can flag hidden spread in womb cancer. Cancer cells entering nearby lymph or blood vessel spaces worsen outlook, yet the sign appears only after surgery.

Records for 156 patients with endometrioid womb cancer treated by standard staging surgery were reviewed. Three inflammation ratios drawn from routine blood counts were kept as plain numbers rather than cut points. The platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio predicted vessel space invasion on its own, while tumor width predicted it even more strongly. A chart tool built from the model may guide surgical planning.
pmc-13304525:
Linhan Li and co-authors design cheek-sticking tablets that release a pain drug in two phases in a 2026 pharmacy study. Indomethacin dissolves poorly, breaks down in stomach acid, and needs both fast relief and lasting cover.

A freeze-dried dispersion raised the drug's dissolving speed many times over the plain powder. Two-layer tablets pressed from powders were tuned for grip and release. The best version freed a large share within twenty minutes, then kept releasing across eight hours while clinging inside the cheek for about as long. Polymer gel behavior and tablet wear govern the balance struck.
pmc-13304925:
Lisa Khairil leads a 2026 narrative review questioning whether artificial intelligence has truly improved drug discovery outcomes. Investment passed one hundred billion dollars in recent years, yet roughly nine in ten drug candidates still fail after entering human testing.

Star tools predict protein shapes with near-lab accuracy, but they falter on protein motion, chemical tags, and drug binding detail. Case studies show faster early work without matching gains in late-stage success. Weak repeatability, hidden data, and patchy regulation add risk. Stronger proof standards and shared data are urged before hype becomes trust.
pmc-13305325:
Alessandro Di Minno leads a 2026 randomized trial of a mixed-fiber blend for adults with functional constipation. Laxatives are standard care but do not suit everyone, and pairing fibers from several food sources might work better than one alone.

Fifty-four adults took two sachets daily of the blend or a placebo for 28 days in a blinded design. The blend mixed wheat dextrin, fruit pectin, citrus fibers, and oat fibers. Bowel movements rose clearly by week four, and stool form returned to normal from week two. Bloating, swelling, heaviness, and gas all eased, with no side effects reported.
pmc-13307025:
Liang Qi proposed confusing aircraft radar-cancelling systems with two separated jammers in a 2026 study. Random phase jumps between the pair swing the combined wavefront direction fast, breaking the steady null such systems track.

Simulations cut the average cancellation ratio from 26.80 dB to 20.29 dB, a drop of 6.51 dB in reported figures. Timing and phase errors between the jammers barely dented the effect in the same runs. The authors present the scheme as a lean way to gain direction agility without precise transmission control. Two linked sources are enough, which keeps cost and set up work low in use.
pmc-13307725:
Giulia Congedo and co-authors survey in 2026 what staff at an Italian university hospital know and feel about the pneumococcal vaccine, which guards older and at risk adults. Their survey ran from February to June 2024 and drew both health workers and office staff at the Gemelli hospital.

Cover was low in both groups, at 20 percent for health staff and 19 percent for office staff in the survey. Health staff knew more, while office staff showed more doubt and less awareness of the vaccine. Both groups favoured shots given at work and asked for clear teaching sessions. Doctors trusted the vaccine most, and they also advised family to take it far more often.
pmc-13307825:
Domenico Antonio Restivo and co-authors present in 2026 three cases of laryngeal adductor breathing dystonia, a rare nerve driven spasm that narrows the voice box during breathing in. Unlike the better known voice form, this form leaves speech mostly intact and instead blocks airflow, which can mimic other throat block causes.

All three cases mixed the usual throat signs with spasms in nearby head districts, which widens the known range of the condition. Standard retraining, speech work, and most drugs help little in true cases of this kind. Botulinum toxin shots into the throat muscles eased the harsh breathing noise in chosen patients, so exact typing of each case guides who should get that targeted care.
pmc-13308225:
Alvin E Lirio and co-authors run in 2026 the first gene study of asthma in a Filipino group, testing known variants in mothers from the Cebu survey cohort. Among 1678 unrelated mothers, 129 told of asthma, and 27 variants drawn from large global studies were checked one by one and as a joint score.

One variant in the SMAD3 gene passed the strict bar, with an odds ratio of 1.80 for asthma in this group. The joint score also tracked with higher odds, though the gain per step was small in size. Small numbers barred a full genome scan, so the authors call for more cohorts in groups that gene studies have long skipped over.
pmc-13308725:
Chenyang Huang and co-authors test in 2026 whether a lower oestrogen dose can hold pregnancy rates in hormone primed frozen embryo transfer cycles. Records from 2022 to mid 2025 split 1955 high dose cycles from 202 low dose cycles, all with one blastocyst moved per cycle.

Raw rates favoured the low dose group, yet the groups differed in age and egg reserve at the start of care. After matching and model fixes, the gap shrank and lost firm standing in the final checks. Early loss rates also matched between groups. A gentler dose may suit younger women, yet forward trials must prove the trade is safe and fair.
pmc-13309525:
Shinji Futami and co-authors study harmful self-directed antibodies in a rare lung disease in a 2026 article. In autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, antibodies attack a signal the lungs need to clear fatty material, yet total antibody amount does not match how sick patients are. The team asked whether the exact target spot and grip strength matter more.

From 28 patients, 186 antibodies were sorted by which spot on the signal they bind. For one binding class, tighter grip meant stronger blocking, and patients with more of these antibodies were sicker. High-grip antibodies of that class alone caused disease signs in engineered mice. The authors say target spot plus grip, not amount alone, drives harm.
pmc-13311125:
Carolynn Hare and colleagues test whether autistic and ADHD traits shape how senses combine in a 2026 study. Both conditions show sense processing differences, and they often co-occur, yet joint trait effects were unclear. A broad university sample did a fast detection task that measures gain from paired sights and sounds.

Ninety two young adults took part, with a mean age near 18 years old at testing. Trait scores showed no link to accuracy gain from paired senses. No added or joint effect of the two trait sets appeared either. When base sense sharpness is held equal, trait level alone may not drive sense combining in young adults.
pmc-13311725:
Henry Badji and co-authors lay out protocols in a 2026 article for using genome sequencing to trace gut bacteria that cause diarrhea across Africa. The GETCampy-Africa study sits inside a One Health frame.

Standard lab work shows where these germs are but cannot resolve fine strain differences, drug resistance, or spread paths. The study uses a case-control design across several countries, sampling people, animals, and the environment. Genome data will pin down which sources feed human illness and how strains move. The protocols give other teams a shared method for high-resolution gut germ tracking.
pmc-13311925:
Seungyoon Roh and co-authors in 2026 present a study on how three Toll-like receptor paths shape the inflammatory output of chicken macrophages. The cytokine IL-1 beta sits at the center of the network.

The team stimulated a chicken macrophage cell line and blood-derived macrophages through the TLR2, TLR3, and TLR4 routes. Responses differed sharply by route, with the virus-mimic route raising IL-1 beta, IL-18, and interferon beta, while the bacterial wall route answered weakly. A gene-edited line lacking IL-1 beta let the team test how the cytokine steers each route's output. The work fills a gap in bird immunology with disease-control value.
pmc-13312025:
Peishuang He and colleagues use computer models and multi-omics data in a 2027 study to explain why retinol speeds cell growth at low doses yet harms cells at high ones. Retinol is a common anti-aging ingredient in skin products, but the switch behind this two-way behavior was unclear.

Working with human foreskin fibroblasts, the team combined gene, protein, and metabolite data with a genome-scale metabolic model. Low doses switched on retinoic acid signaling and rerouted cell chemistry in ways that favor growth. High doses instead brought oxidative stress, a build-up of harmful intermediates, and signs of ferroptosis, a form of cell death. The authors name control points such as DHRS3 and GCLM that could guide safer retinol products.
pmc-13312825:
Azadeh Rakhshan and colleagues present a 2026 case report of ossifying fasciitis in a man's hand, a benign growth notorious for impersonating cancer. The lesion mixes spindle-cell growth with stray bone formation and grows fast enough, with dense imaging, to be mistaken for a sarcoma. While it usually appears on the trunk or upper limbs, the hand is an exceptionally rare site.

Their patient, aged 34, developed a painless lump on the palm of his right hand over two months, sitting beside a flexor tendon on scans. Under the microscope the removed mass showed fibroblasts in bundles within loose stroma, bone rimmed by osteoblasts, and scattered giant cells, with no malignant features. Marker tests confirmed the diagnosis. The authors stress that knowing this entity, and matching tissue, imaging, and clinical clues, spares patients needless radical surgery.
pmc-13313525:
Luana Figueiredo and Makeda Smith host a conversation piece, published in 2026, on how Canada should think about national and human security. Experts in defense studies, foreign policy, law, and human rights weigh the costs of guarding sovereignty. They also weigh the weakness of shared alliances in a shifting world.

The piece weighs the risk of American indifference or hostility. It notes a turn toward ad hoc coalitions, whole-society defense models, and strength at home. It also shows how border rules and selective law use can repeat racialized harm and wear down humane norms. The authors argue that Canada cannot outsource its safety or rest it on arms alone. Real security must rest on justice, equity, and human rights. Guarding the state means little if people inside it are not safe and free.
pmc-13314425:
Qingping Zhang leads a 2026 study of whether living high on a plateau dulls hearing. Long-term life at altitude has been floated as a factor in hearing, but proof from people who live high for years was limited.

The study drew 187 plateau residents aged 50 years or less at a Qinghai hospital health check. They were split by home altitude into three groups. The low group held 79 people at 2200 to 2499 meters. The middle group held 51 at 2500 to 3499 meters, and the high group held 57 at 3500 meters or more, by the report counts. Hearing was tested at six tones from 250 Hz to 8 kHz in both ears, with averages for low and high tones too. Early results showed the clearest group gaps at the high tones. The work weighs altitude as a quiet risk for the ears of plateau peoples.
pmc-13314625:
Ângela Alves, Rita Pombinho, and Didier Cabanes review how single-cell methods expose variety in bacterial virulence, in a 2026 paper. Cloned bacteria do not act as one uniform mass; during infection they split into unlike states across place and time.

That spread springs from random gene firing, shifting surroundings, gene change, and cell aging, the authors write. Tricks such as two-state switches, phase variation, dormant persistence, quorum sensing, and memory of past states let cells hedge bets and share labor. Groups gain fitness and staying power in hostile hosts by mixing bold and quiet members. Single-cell tools can now decode this patchwork gene by gene. Grasping it may explain why infections flare or linger and where new drugs could strike.
pmc-13315325:
C Parisi and a large oncology team report in 2026 on sex differences in side effects from new antibody-drug conjugates for lung cancer. Patients with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer got these drugs in early-phase trials at Gustave Roussy between 2018 and 2023, targeting proteins such as TROP2, HER2, and others.

Among 132 patients, about half women, three quarters had side effects of grade 2 or worse. Women had more such effects than men, with 82.8 percent affected versus 69.1 percent for men, and a higher median count of effects. Metabolic problems such as appetite loss and weight loss were also more common in women.
pmc-13316225:
Yi Lin sets out in 2026 a perspective on plant embodied intelligence, the idea that adaptive problem solving in plants emerges from the interplay of their spread-out structures with the environment. Intelligence is increasingly discussed beyond brains and nerves, and this branch of the idea was still undeveloped.

The review lays foundations and research paths, from shape change and growth to distributed memory, ecological signaling, swarm-like behavior, and decisions under risk. Global work spans plant neurobiology, systems biology, and bio-inspired materials. Mixing careful measurement, molecular tools, ecology models, and plant-inspired robots could advance both plant and intelligent systems science.
pmc-13316625:
Tristan N Samuels and colleagues built a 2026 human cell model for a rare inherited disease caused by faulty copies of NARS1, a gene needed to charge transfer RNA with asparagine. The illness strikes infants and children, hits the nervous system, and has no targeted treatment.

Two dominant faulty copies made cells sicken and switch on a stress program. Adding plain asparagine fully restored growth in patient skin cells and shut the stress signal off, a rescue the team also saw across protein patterns. A matching transfer RNA therapy and a stress-blocking drug each helped only in part. The simple nutrient result points to a low-cost treatment lead worth clinical testing.
pmc-13318725:
Ziyan Lyu and colleagues present a 2026 expert consensus on running combined cardio-oncology clinics. These clinics pair cardiologists with clinical pharmacists. Their shared task is safe, rational drug use in cancer patients. Heart damage from anticancer drugs is a leading cause of death in this group.

No established management systems existed for such joint clinics. Sichuan Provincial People's Hospital therefore led the effort, sponsored by the Clinical Pharmacy Branch. That hospital opened its combined clinic in March 2022. The consensus responds to national policy promoting pharmacist-led services and medication counselling. It aims to standardise workflows and pharmaceutical care for cardio-oncology patients. Single-discipline care, the authors argue, cannot meet these complex needs alone.
pmc-13319925:
Erik Stuchlý and co-authors test how people guess the choices of others in a 2026 study of mental copying. When we forecast what a friend will pick, we may run our own choice process in our head as a stand in. If that inner process is skewed, the forecast should skew too, a claim the team tested by first bending risk tastes.

People were tuned to high or low chance settings, which shifted their own risk values, then asked to forecast picks by three stock figures with set risk styles. Their forecasts shifted for the average and risk shy figures but not for the risk seeking one. Own risk lean also tracked forecasts for the first two figures only. Copying seems real, but who the other person is sets its limits.
pmc-13320325:
Ben-Jian Zhong and co-authors name three new mushroom species from subtropical China in a 2026 taxonomy study. The trio belongs to a brittlegill group known for mild taste and varied cap colors, sorted here by both looks and gene proof. Field finds from the region were checked spore by spore and joined to gene trees built from four gene zones.

One new species wears a dark ruby grey cap with tight gills and flesh that stays white when bruised. The second wears a pale pink white cap and a stem that yellows with age or bruising. The third shifts from red grey to purple brown and its flesh browns when bruised. Gene trees back all three as fresh branches, and full accounts with photos fix their names for future finds.
pmc-13320425:
Yuan-Qing Luo and co-authors turn roasted sesame hulls into a flavor boost for sesame oil in a 2026 food study. Hulls are a thrown away part of the seed, yet roasting loads them with prized scent compounds. Soaking hulls in plain oil was tuned to draw that scent across while also testing whether the hull goods slow oil spoilage in storage.

The best soak used one part hull to five parts oil at mild heat for eight hours, in the trials reported. That oil gained balanced caramel, roast, and nut notes from hull aromatics. In fast aged storage its spoilage marks first rose faster, then after forty days climbed far more slowly than plain oil, and off scent build up stayed lower. Waste hulls thus serve twice, as flavor and as guard.
pmc-13320825:
Bo Pan leads a large expert group setting out a staging system for children's heart function in a 2026 guidance article. Heart failure in children is rising worldwide, and the group, from the Pediatrics Society of the Chinese Medical Association, wants care to start earlier in the disease course. The system applies to all children, not only those already ill.

Three stages are defined, from full heart function through early dysfunction to outright failure. For each stage, the article sets out how to recognise it and how to manage it, forming a full care pathway. The stated aim is to make childhood heart failure more preventable and treatable and to cut its long term burden.
pmc-13321225:
Alshaimaa Tarek and colleagues report a rare artery disease found before birth in a 2026 case report from Egypt. Generalized arterial calcification of infancy hardens and narrows large arteries very early in life, often causing breathing distress, heart failure, and high blood pressure. About 300 cases have been reported worldwide.

At 29 weeks of pregnancy, ultrasound showed valve narrowing, thickened heart walls, and heavy calcium in the aorta and ductal arch of the fetus. Gene testing found a homozygous harmful change in the ENPP1 gene, written as c.749C>T in the report. The authors call it the first gene confirmed Egyptian fetal case and stress expert heart scanning plus gene tests for counselling.
pmc-13322625:
Taynara Gabriele Ribeiro Piano and co-authors test selenium and tellurium compounds against gut worms of farm animals in a 2026 laboratory study. Roundworm infections harm ruminant health, and heavy dewormer use breeds resistant parasites. Three compounds were tested on worm eggs and larvae from sheep and cattle, with cell safety checks alongside.

One selenium compound, diphenyl diselenide, stopped egg hatching best, while the tellurium compound AS-101 killed larvae best in the assays. Pairing the selenium compound with ivermectin gave a mild joint boost. That selenium compound was also gentlest on kidney cells in culture. The results mark a possible new family of worm treatments for livestock.
pmc-13322825:
Haoyu Wen, Weiwei Chen and Yuquan He explain how blood vessel walls harden with calcium, in a 2026 review of vascular calcification. The process is now seen as active, driven by smooth muscle cells in the vessel wall rather than simple mineral build-up.

Under strain from calcium and phosphate imbalance, sugar and fat toxicity, oxidative stress and long-term inflammation, those cells switch toward a bone-like state. They release tiny vesicles, break down surrounding matrix and switch on growth signals such as Wnt and BMP pathways. Other cell changes add to the effect. The authors discuss treatment ideas that target metabolic control points, block the cell switch, or alter gene regulation.
pmc-13323025:
Matteo Ricchi and a large team develop a counting method for Salmonella Infantis in poultry faeces, reported in 2026. This serovar dominates broiler production in the European Union and often colonises birds without signs, letting resistant strains spread quietly into meat.

Their method adapts a miniaturised most-probable-number approach and confirms results with a specific qPCR test. Performance checks used spiked and naturally contaminated samples, with matrix effects judged by Bland-Altman analysis and repeat testing across runs and operators. Applied to real samples, the method quantified bacterial loads well enough for risk assessment work. The authors present it as a monitoring tool for flock-level control in Italy and beyond.
pmc-13323125:
Huixian Xie and co-authors test a structured weight programme for psychiatric inpatients, in a 2026 study at Taizhou Second People's Hospital. Their 5-4-3 model joins five fields, four phases and three supports in one loop. Psychiatry, nursing, nutrition, rehab and pharmacy staff lead it jointly.

Inpatients with a body mass index of 24 or higher joined between November 2024 and April 2025. Care ran through stays of one to six months. A three-month follow-up came after discharge. Outcomes covered weight, body mass index and metabolic measures. They also covered patient knowledge and staff practice. Weight after discharge came mainly from self-report, which the authors flag as a bias risk.
pmc-13323325:
Rodolfo G Gatto, Hossam Youssef and Yuen Gao introduce a collection on imaging biomarkers for TDP-43 and tau protein diseases, in a 2026 editorial. The two abnormal proteins recur across many degenerative brain disorders and increasingly look like partners rather than separate problems.

Tau tangles and TDP-43 clumps can drive each other's build-up, harm synapses and disturb RNA handling, jointly speeding neuron loss in the editors' framing. Structural MRI shows shrinkage patterns while PET imaging traces molecular pathology in living brain. Featured work adds further clinical dimensions beyond classic symptoms. The editors argue that imaging both proteins together is key to earlier and sharper diagnosis of these mixed diseases.
pmc-13325125:
Soroush Torkamannejad, Hoi-ying Yip, and Bingyun Sun count heart ion channel proteins directly in a 2026 proteomics study. These large membrane channels set the heartbeat rhythm, and faulty levels can trigger dangerous arrhythmias.

Targeted parallel reaction monitoring with an in-sample calibration method measured copy numbers in human ventricle tissue. Extended digestion of the tough tissue fraction exposed proteins that broad surveys miss. The team quantified the main subunits Nav1.5, hERG, and Cav1.2, plus the helpers Cavβ1 and Cavα2δ1. Copy numbers let labs compare channel counts across studies and hearts on the same scale. The method should extend to systematic surveys of these hard-to-measure proteins.
pmc-13325625:
Daniele Midori Kakimoto Higa and colleagues review anesthesia for balloon heart valve repair in dogs in a 2026 retrospective study. Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty eases severe pulmonic stenosis, but the strained heart makes anesthesia risky.

Records covered 21 dogs treated in 2024 and 2025, with a median age of 18 months. French Bulldogs made up 33.3 percent of cases, and fainting was the top sign at 42.9 percent of the dogs. Induction leaned on etomidate and midazolam in 95 percent of procedures. Low blood pressure struck 66.7 percent of dogs during surgery and often needed drug support. The balloon cut the valve gradient in 90 percent of cases.
pmc-13326425:
Fatima Gul and colleagues relate blood branched-chain amino acids to body fat in visceral obesity in a 2026 study. Belly fat ties closely to insulin resistance, yet the place of these amino acids in that link is unsettled.

The study enrolled 105 people: 52 with obesity alone, 32 with obesity plus type 2 diabetes, and 21 healthy controls. Amino acid levels ran higher in both obesity groups, with valine up most, at 43.46 micrograms per mL in the diabetes group against 30.48 in controls. Levels tracked with visceral fat area, waist size, and insulin resistance scores. Valine showed the tightest links and stayed tied to waist size in joint models.
pmc-13327025:
Yunwei Long and colleagues report a 2026 surgical series for Kümmell's disease, where a spinal bone collapses weeks after injury and bends the back. Common cement procedures often fail in late stages, so the team tested short-segment fixation paired with a leverage method to straighten the spine.

Records covered 22 patients treated from 2020 to 2023, with pain scores, nerve function grades, and spinal measurements compared before and after surgery. Operations averaged about 100 minutes with modest blood loss, pain eased, and restored bone height reached 83 percent of expected values on average, alongside a mean angle correction of 19.32 degrees across the group. Nerve grades also improved, supporting the combined approach for advanced cases.
pmc-13328025:
Krystyna Kowalczuk and colleagues measure skipped nursing care across three countries in a 2026 survey. Care rationing, leaving needed tasks undone, lowers quality and raises error risk. Between March 2024 and March 2025, 610 hospital nurses in the Czech Republic, Poland, and Slovakia rated how often 32 nursing activities were omitted.

Both the energy chain's complex I and mitochondrial fusion are needed for differentiation, but their interplay was unknown. Cutting complex I parts left stem cell counts intact yet shrank their lineages and slowed growth.

Damaged energy chains raised reactive oxygen, lowered membrane power, and muted a key growth signal in offspring cells. Blocking the fusion brake restored oxygen balance, growth, and maturation in the depleted cells. Antioxidant support and stronger growth signaling also rescued the defects, which ties fusion and complex I into one control circuit.
pmc-13387625:
Zachary J. Tucker and Jason Boardman report three port-site hernias after robot-assisted hernia repair in a 2026 case report. A 69-year-old man had mesh repair of an umbilical hernia through three 8 mm robotic ports left without fascial closure. Two weeks later he reported a new lump at the lowest port site.

Scans confirmed a fat-containing hernia there, and surgery 32 days after the first operation found hernias at all three port sites. The fatty omentum sat inside each, trapped at the largest, which measured 2 cm across in the report. The case questions whether small robotic ports can safely skip closure.
pmc-13388325:
Andrew Mente argues against strict low-sodium targets for whole populations in a 2026 counterpoint review. Many guidelines urge intake below 2.3 grams per day, expecting lower blood pressure and fewer heart events. Mente contends that hard outcome evidence for such low levels is lacking, and that keeping diets that low in real life has no proven method.

Most people eat a moderate 3 to 5 grams daily, the range tied to the lowest event risk in his reading. He recommends a target below 5 grams instead, pending large trials with clinical endpoints. Sodium from medicines, not just food, should count in personal advice.
pmc-13389425:
Joyeeta Mandal and co-authors validate, in 2026, a standard reporting system for lymph node needle samples in a region where tuberculosis is common. The Sydney System sorts these samples into five levels meant to guide care by the risk of cancer at each level.

The team reviewed 427 cases from two large hospitals in eastern India during 2025, with three pathologists scoring slides separately and without clinical details. Tissue results and a stain for tuberculosis bacteria served as the reference. Most samples came from neck nodes, and reactive, granulomatous, and necrotising patterns were common. Pathologists gain local accuracy figures, cancer risk by level, and agreement scores that show whether the system works fairly where tuberculosis often mimics cancer.
pmc-13391725:
Shrinit Babel and colleagues systematically review, in 2026, liquid biopsy based on extracellular vesicles for detecting cancer spread to the membranes around the brain and spinal cord. Leptomeningeal metastasis is a devastating complication of systemic cancers with poor outlook and difficult diagnosis.

Searching several databases to January 2025, the team appraised studies of vesicle-carried markers, such as microRNAs and proteins, in spinal fluid or blood for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment monitoring. Cancer doctors gain a sharp review of a new path. It could spare patients repeat spinal taps and cell checks. The gaps that must close first are set out in plain terms, so labs know what proof is still owed. Spinal fluid gives the best yield, the review finds, since the fluid bathes the site of spread.
pmc-13392625:
Bishal Khaniya leads a team reporting a twin pregnancy in which one twin had no working heart and survived only because blood flowed backward to it from its healthy partner. The rare pattern is called TRAP sequence. The mother was thirty years old and in her third pregnancy. Ultrasound in the middle trimester picked up the malformed twin, which had no head.

Because the healthy twin showed no sign of heart strain or fluid overload, the team chose watchful waiting over intervention. Pregnancy carried on to thirty-eight weeks, when a planned caesarean delivered the pair. The authors argue that careful monitoring alone can be the right call when the pumping twin stays stable, reserving procedures for cases showing early compromise.
pmc-13392825:
Giuliana Pavone and four co-authors review how doctors might predict which women with advanced or returning womb cancer will respond to immunotherapy. Drugs that release immune brakes have transformed care for tumours with faulty DNA repair. That group is flagged by mismatch repair deficiency and high microsatellite instability. The drugs now feature even in first-line plans. Yet some women in that favoured group still fail to respond, for reasons nobody has pinned down.

Markers that guide treatment in other cancers, including mutation load and PD-L1 staining, behave inconsistently in womb cancer. The larger group whose repair systems work normally remains the harder problem, although a minority there respond too. Candidate signals tied to TP53, BRCA, and a DNA repair weakness called HRD have all been tested without yielding a dependable test. The review maps what trials would need to settle the question.
pmc-13393725:
Tim Van Den Bossche leads a twenty-five-author progress report on the Metaproteomics Initiative. The community network launched in 2021 for scientists who catalogue all proteins across whole microbial communities at once. The field had grown fast without shared standards, and the network set out to align benchmarks, reporting norms, and training. Five years on, the authors take stock and look ahead.

The network has run shared benchmark studies, helped shape metadata and reporting standards, produced hands-on guidance and teaching materials, and staged global symposia linking the wider microbiome world. Its next push, called the Grand Metaproteome Challenges, aims at joint, field-wide projects spanning health, factory, and nature questions. The authors invite the broader omics community to join, crediting steady volunteer teamwork with maturing the field.
pmc-13394025:
Toan Pham dissected heart muscle from type 2 diabetic rats to find why its mitochondria, the cell's power stations, falter, testing the parts separately on carbohydrate and fatty acid fuels. Metabolite profiling by mass spectrometry ran beside measures of respiration, energy flux, corrosive oxygen output, and membrane voltage in heart tissue. Diabetes was expected to blunt everything, but the defect proved choosy.

On carbohydrate fuel, diabetic mitochondria breathed, produced energy, and held voltage as well as healthy ones. On fatty acids, respiration and energy flux dropped sharply even though the muscle was swimming in fatty acid species, several of them plainly piled up. Krebs cycle intermediates barely moved. Pham reads the pattern as metabolic inflexibility: fuel oversupply unmatched by burning capacity, wasting energy promise in the diabetic heart.
pmc-13394925:
Alexandra V. Jürs and colleagues compare, in 2026, young and adult cases of ALS tied to the FUS gene. ALS wastes the nerve cells that drive movement. Three patients whose illness began before age 25 were set against adult-onset cases. The team tested thinking skills, verbal scores, brain scans, and sugar-use scans.

The young cases worsened fast and showed broad thinking deficits plus low verbal scores from early life. Their scans showed shrinkage and low activity at the back of the brain. Adult cases kept more volume and had milder, more typical changes. The authors read the pattern as a growth delay, not just decay. They back gene checks for young patients with learning limits.
pmc-13395225:
Jason Silvestre and co-authors trace, in 2026, the training path for sleep doctors in the United States. Warnings of a coming shortfall frame the study. The team read match data for sleep fellowships from 2012 to 2025. They counted applicants, training posts, and posts left empty each year.

Applicants grew faster than posts over the span, rising well over twofold. Empty posts fell from about one in eight to one in twenty. Graduates of United States medical schools won places at higher rates than peers trained abroad. Their share of new fellows also rose. The authors urge close watch on match trends as need for sleep care climbs.
pmc-13395325:
Joanna Yang and colleagues tune, in 2026, the DNA rings used to deliver genes into liver and brain cancer cells. Polymer specks carry the rings, but ring design shapes how well genes switch on. The team built fourteen ring variants that swap promoter, backbone, size, and selection marker. They tested glow genes in six liver cancer lines and three brain cancer lines.

One promoter, CMV, beat its rivals in the same backbone. The smallest ring, with no antibiotic marker, lit the most cells and glowed brightest in most liver lines. Smaller rings trended better overall. The authors say lean ring design should guide future gene drugs. Skipping drug markers also eases safety review.
pmc-13395425:
Roschelle L. Fritz and co-authors evaluate, in 2026, a community-wrapped smart home system for older adults living alone. Sensors watched movement in the homes of 48 older adults with chronic illness and low income for six months. Alerts fired when daily patterns shifted. Notices climbed a ladder from the resident to family, community workers, and nurses.

The sensors logged tens of millions of readings, boiled down to thousands of alerts. Residents answered few email alerts, and more of the text follow-ups.
